title: Circuit words: components, series and parallel
keyIdea: Each part of a circuit is a component. A cell gives the push, called voltage; a battery is two or more cells joined. Current is the flow of electricity, and it only flows round a complete circuit, a loop of conductors with no gaps. A switch opens and closes a gap. In a series circuit everything sits in one loop, so extra bulbs add resistance, every bulb is dimmer and one gap stops them all. In a parallel circuit each bulb has its own branch, so each is as bright as one bulb alone and the others stay on if one is removed.

kid: A circuit is a loop that electricity flows round. Each part of it is a component. A cell gives the push. Two or more cells joined make a battery. A bulb gives light, a buzzer makes a sound and a motor spins. Wires join them up.

The flow is called current. The push from the cell is the voltage. Current only flows round a complete circuit. That means a full loop with no gaps, from one end of the cell, through the parts, and back to the other end. Wires are made of metal because metals are conductors. Plastic is an insulator, so it blocks the flow.
A switch is a gap you can control. When it is closed, the circuit is complete and the bulb lights. When it is open, there is a gap, so the bulb goes off. Open does not let the electricity out.

In a series circuit all the parts are in one loop. Add a second bulb and both get dimmer, because two bulbs give more resistance and less current flows. Take one bulb out and they all go off. In a parallel circuit each bulb has its own branch. Each one is as bright as one bulb alone, and if one goes out, the rest stay on.
adult: This lesson matches the English national curriculum for Year 4 Electricity: children should 'construct a simple series electrical circuit, identifying and naming its basic parts, including cells, wires, bulbs, switches and buzzers', and 'recognise that a switch opens and closes a circuit'. It also adds the Year 6 idea that brightness depends on the number of cells and bulbs, and the words series and parallel.

The key terms are component, cell, battery, current, voltage, resistance, conductor, insulator, switch, complete circuit, series and parallel. In everyday speech a single AA cell is called a battery. In science a battery is two or more cells joined, and the cell is the single unit.

Common mistakes: thinking one wire from the cell is enough, thinking an open switch lets the current through, and thinking the bulb uses up the current. Another slip is to believe that a second bulb in series gets the same current as one bulb alone. In fact both bulbs are dimmer. In parallel each branch gets the full voltage of the cell, so each bulb is as bright as one alone, but the cell gives more current in total and runs down faster.

In the lab your learner finds six components by name, closes two gaps to make a complete circuit and works a switch. Then they add a second bulb in series and in parallel and unscrew one, to see which bulbs stay on. Please be careful at home: mains electricity is never used for experiments, only small cells.

familyTip: Look at a set of fairy lights or a torch together. Ask: is there a switch? Where does it make a gap? If one fairy light goes out and the rest stay on, are the bulbs in series or in parallel? Count the cells in a torch or a remote and talk about why more cells give a bigger push.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find six components, close the gaps to complete a circuit, work a switch, then add a second bulb in series and in parallel and unscrew one.

practice.prompt: Which word means two or more cells joined together?
practice.hint: One cell gives a push. Join cells and you get a bigger push.
practice.explain: A battery is two or more cells joined together. One single unit on its own is a cell.

practice.prompt: A parallel circuit has {a} bulbs, each on its own branch. You unscrew {b} of them. How many bulbs stay lit?
practice.hint: In parallel each bulb has its own complete branch. Only the unscrewed ones go out.
practice.explain: Each branch is its own loop, so only the {b} unscrewed bulbs go out. {a} − {b} = {=a-b} bulbs stay lit.

practice.prompt: A series circuit has {a} bulbs in one loop. One of them is unscrewed. How many bulbs stay lit?
practice.hint: In series there is only one path. What does one gap do to that path?
practice.explain: Unscrewing one bulb makes a gap in the only path, so the current stops and all {a} bulbs go out. 0 stay lit.

practice.prompt: A circuit has a cell, a bulb and an open switch. What does the bulb do?
practice.hint: An open switch makes a gap. Can the current get round?
practice.explain: An open switch makes a gap, so the circuit is not complete. No current flows and the bulb stays off.

pool.prompt: What must a circuit have for current to flow?
choices: a complete loop with no gaps
one wire from the cell to the bulb
pool.hint: Trace the path from one end of the cell back to the other end.
pool.explain: Current only flows round a complete circuit: a full loop from one end of the cell, through the parts, back to the other end.

pool.prompt: Which component changes electrical energy into sound?
pool.hint: Think of a door bell or an alarm.
pool.explain: A buzzer changes electrical energy into sound. A motor gives movement, and a cell gives the push.

pool.prompt: You add a second bulb in series with the first. What happens?
pool.hint: Two bulbs in one loop give more resistance.
pool.explain: In series the two bulbs share one path. More resistance means less current, so both are dimmer.

pool.prompt: In a house, one light can be off while the others are on. How are the lights wired?
pool.hint: Which kind of circuit lets one bulb go out while the rest stay on?
pool.explain: They are in parallel: each light has its own branch and switch, so one can be off while the others stay on.

pool.prompt: Why are wires made of copper with a plastic coat?
pool.hint: Which one is a metal, and what do metals do to current?
pool.explain: Copper is a metal, so it is a good conductor and carries the current. Plastic is an insulator, so it keeps the current off your hands.

pool.prompt: What does the voltage of a cell tell you?
choices: how big a push it gives
pool.hint: The cell pushes the current round the loop.
pool.explain: Voltage is the size of the push the cell gives. A bigger voltage pushes more current through the same bulb, so it glows brighter.

pool.prompt: Fairy lights have {a} bulbs in parallel. {b} bulbs are broken. How many still shine?
pool.hint: In parallel a broken bulb only stops its own branch.
pool.explain: Each bulb has its own branch, so only the {b} broken ones are dark. {a} − {b} = {=a-b} still shine.

pool.prompt: A battery is made of {a} cells joined in a row. How many cells do {b} of these batteries have?
pool.hint: Each battery has {a} cells. Count them for every battery.
